claims.text: Profitability is the ability of a business to earn profit: revenue that is greater than the total costs of earning it, measured over a trading period and expressed in a currency such as Namibian dollars.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A profitable business is more likely to survive and keep growing, because profit rewards the owners for the risk they took, funds expansion without borrowing, and signals that customers value the output at prices above its full cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profitability and cash are not the same: profit is revenue less total costs over a period, while cash is the money actually available to pay bills on a given day, and the timing of credit sales means a profitable business can still run short of cash.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Liquidity is the ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, using the cash and near-cash assets it holds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business that lacks liquidity may be unable to pay suppliers, wages or loan interest on time, so it may lose supplier credit, see workers leave or be forced to raise money quickly - outcomes that can close a business even while it is profitable, because profit and cash-flow are not the same thing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Liquidity is usually judged with two ratios taken from the statement of financial position: the current ratio, which compares all current assets with current liabilities, and the acid test ratio, which removes inventory because inventory may be slow to turn into cash.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The gross profit margin is gross profit expressed as a percentage of revenue: it is calculated as (gross profit divided by revenue) x 100, where gross profit is revenue less the cost of the goods sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rising gross profit margin usually means the business is trading better - selling at higher prices or buying inputs more cheaply - while a falling one usually means input costs are rising faster than the prices customers accept, so each sale leaves a smaller share of revenue as gross profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The gross profit margin ignores operating expenses such as wages, rent and marketing: it measures trading performance only, so a business with a strong gross profit margin can still record a loss once every other cost has been paid.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The profit margin is profit expressed as a percentage of revenue: it is calculated as (profit divided by revenue) x 100, and unlike the gross profit margin it takes every expense into account.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The gross profit margin and the profit margin are different measures: the first subtracts only the cost of the goods sold, while the second subtracts every expense, so a wide gap between them shows the business carries heavy operating expenses relative to its trading profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can improve its profit margin by selling at better prices, buying inputs more cheaply, or reducing operating expenses such as rent and wages, because each route raises the share of revenue that remains as profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) is profit expressed as a percentage of capital employed, calculated as (profit divided by capital employed) x 100, where capital employed here means the long-term funds invested in the business - owner's equity plus non-current liabilities - and not capital goods, which are a factor of production, and not money capital in general.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A ROCE above the rate a bank pays on savings suggests the business is using its long-term funds productively, while a low ROCE suggests the funds might earn more elsewhere, which is why the ratio is usually compared with interest rates and with what other businesses achieve.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An investor comparing two businesses is likely to prefer the one with the higher ROCE, because it indicates that each unit of long-term funds is generating more profit; ROCE is therefore a key ratio in the decision to invest.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities, and is normally written in a form such as 2 to 1.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A current ratio below 1 suggests the business may struggle to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, while a very high ratio suggests cash and other current assets are sitting idle instead of being put to work, so both directions of the figure carry information.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Inventory is counted in the current ratio but is usually the slowest current asset to turn into cash, which is why the acid test ratio removes it before comparing current assets with current liabilities.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The acid test ratio is calculated as (current assets less inventory) divided by current liabilities, and it is the stricter test of liquidity because it counts only assets that can be turned into cash quickly.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The current ratio and the acid test ratio differ in one input: the current ratio counts inventory, while the acid test removes it, so a business holding slow-moving stock may look safe on the current ratio yet fail the acid test.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An acid test result below 1 suggests the business is counting on selling its inventory to pay near-term debts, so a firm with slow-moving stock may need to delay purchases, negotiate longer credit or arrange an overdraft before the due dates arrive.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Users of accounts are the people and organisations with an interest in a business's financial results - owners, managers, lenders, suppliers, employees and government - and each user needs different information from the same statements.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each user of accounts focuses on different ratios: a lender or supplier is likely to weigh liquidity ratios such as the acid test, because they show whether short-term debts can be paid, while an owner or investor is likely to weigh profitability ratios such as ROCE and profit margin, because they show the return the business earns.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ratio analysis helps a user of accounts make sense of raw figures by turning them into percentages and proportions that can be compared with earlier years, with other businesses in the same trade, and with the threshold a user has chosen for a decision.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A lender reading a weak acid test ratio is likely to refuse a loan or to demand security and a shorter repayment period, because the ratio suggests the business may not be able to repay on the agreed dates.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An investor deciding whether to buy into a business is likely to compare its ROCE and profit margin with the returns available elsewhere, because the ratios indicate whether the profit earned justifies the price of investing and the risk taken.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A single ratio for a single year is a snapshot: it may reflect one-off events, accounting choices or an unusual trading period, so users of accounts usually weigh several ratios, the trend across years and the business's context before deciding, and two users can read the same results and still decide differently.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
